bips.title: BIP Purpose and Guidelines
bips.summary: Defines the purpose, types, and workflow of Bitcoin Improvement Proposals.
bips.summaryMarkdown:
BIP 1 is the founding document of the Bitcoin Improvement Proposal process. It defines what a BIP is, describes the three BIP categories — Standards Track, Informational, and Process — and establishes the workflow for proposing changes to Bitcoin. The document specifies the required format for BIP submissions, the role of BIP editors, and the status lifecycle (Draft → Accepted → Final, or Rejected/Withdrawn).

This BIP served as the process framework for the Bitcoin development community from 2011 onward. It was later superseded by BIP 2 in 2016, which provided a more detailed and formalized procedure.
bips.impactMarkdown: BIP 1 established the formal process for proposing changes to Bitcoin, enabling community-driven standardization. It laid the groundwork for all subsequent BIPs and remains historically significant as the procedural foundation of Bitcoin development. Without a structured BIP process, coordinating protocol changes across a decentralized developer community would be impractical.

bips.title: BIP process, revised
bips.summary: Revises and replaces the original BIP process with a more detailed and formalized workflow.
bips.summaryMarkdown:
BIP 2 replaces BIP 1 with a more clearly defined BIP process. It refines the BIP workflow, adds explicit guidelines for BIP editors and their responsibilities, and formalizes the process for transferring BIP ownership. It also introduces a dual-licensing requirement (BSD-2-Clause or Open Publication License) for new BIPs.

This BIP was the governing process document from 2016 until its replacement by BIP 3 in 2025.
bips.impactMarkdown: BIP 2 provided a decade of procedural stability for Bitcoin development. By formalizing editor responsibilities, ownership transfers, and licensing requirements, it reduced ambiguity in the BIP process and helped the community scale its standardization efforts as Bitcoin grew.

bips.title: Updated BIP Process
bips.summary: Streamlines the BIP process and clarifies the role and limitations of BIPs within the Bitcoin ecosystem.
bips.summaryMarkdown:
BIP 3 replaces BIP 2 with a streamlined process that addresses lessons learned since 2016. Key changes include reducing the judgment calls assigned to BIP editors, more clearly delineating BIP types, and emphasizing that individual BIPs do not represent community consensus — they represent recommendations by their authors. The BIP also introduces the concept of Deputies (stand-in owners for BIPs) and generalizes the workflow to fit the community's actual use of the repository.

This BIP requires BIP 123 for implementation and represents the current active process as of 2025.
bips.impactMarkdown: BIP 3 modernizes the BIP process for the current era of Bitcoin development. By reducing editor discretion and clarifying that BIPs are author recommendations rather than community consensus documents, it aims to lower barriers to contribution while maintaining quality standards.

bips.title: Version bits with lock-in by height
bips.summary: Proposes an alternative to BIP 9 using block heights instead of timestamps for soft fork activation.
bips.summaryMarkdown:
BIP 8 specifies an alternative to the BIP 9 version bits mechanism for deploying backward-compatible soft forks. Unlike BIP 9 which uses median time past (MTP) timestamps, BIP 8 uses block heights for both the start and timeout of a deployment. It also introduces a `lockinontimeout` parameter that can guarantee activation at the timeout height even without supermajority miner signalling, effectively providing a mandatory flag-day activation path.

The proposal was motivated by concerns that a sudden loss of hashrate could interfere with BIP 9's timestamp-based activation, and that timestamp-based thresholds are less reliable and intuitive than block height thresholds.
bips.impactMarkdown: BIP 8 remains in Draft status but has influenced discussions around soft fork activation mechanisms, particularly during the Taproot activation where BIP 8's LOT=true parameter was debated. While BIP 9 remains the standard approach, BIP 8's insights on lock-in guarantees have shaped community understanding of activation safety.

bips.title: Version bits with timeout and delay
bips.summary: Defines the version bits mechanism for parallel deployment of multiple backward-compatible soft forks.
bips.summaryMarkdown:
BIP 9 introduces a mechanism for deploying multiple soft forks simultaneously by interpreting the nVersion field in block headers as a bit vector. Each bit represents a separate deployment, and activation requires a threshold of miner signalling (typically 95%) within a retarget period. The mechanism includes a timeout after which a failed deployment's bit can be reused.

This BIP has been the primary method for soft fork activation in Bitcoin since 2015, used for deployments including BIP 68 (relative lock-time), BIP 112 (CHECKSEQUENCEVERIFY), BIP 113 (median time past), and BIP 141 (SegWit). It replaced the simpler nVersion-based approach of BIP 34.
bips.impactMarkdown: BIP 9 is one of the most consequential informational BIPs, having enabled the parallel deployment of multiple critical soft forks without coordination conflicts. Its bit-vector design allowed SegWit and other upgrades to proceed independently, and the timeout mechanism prevents stalled deployments from permanently occupying bits.

bips.title: Multi-Sig Transaction Distribution
bips.summary: Standardizes the encoding and distribution of multi-signature transaction proposals.
bips.summaryMarkdown:
BIP 10 defines a standard format for encoding proposed multi-signature transactions — called a Transaction Distribution Proposal (TxDP) — to facilitate signature collection and broadcasting among multiple parties. The format includes the serialized transaction with blank signature scripts, the full previous transactions for verification without blockchain access, and a structured mechanism for collecting and combining signatures.

The goal is to guarantee interoperability between different wallet and signing implementations when handling multi-signature transactions.
bips.impactMarkdown: While BIP 10 provides a well-designed standard for multisig transaction distribution, it saw limited adoption as simpler multisig approaches (BIP 11, BIP 16) gained wider implementation. It remains relevant as a reference for offline signing workflows and air-gapped key management systems.

bips.title: M-of-N Standard Transactions
bips.summary: Proposes M-of-N multi-signature transactions as a new standard transaction type using OP_CHECKMULTISIG.
bips.summaryMarkdown:
BIP 11 introduces standard transactions requiring M-of-N signatures using the existing OP_CHECKMULTISIG opcode. The proposal limits n to 3 or fewer for standard relay. It increases the maximum standard scriptSig size from 200 to 500 bytes to accommodate multi-signature transactions.

Use cases include wallet protection services (2-of-2) and three-party escrow (2-of-3). This BIP was implemented in the Bitcoin Core client and remains a fundamental building block for multi-signature wallets.
bips.impactMarkdown: BIP 11 was the first standard to enable multi-signature transactions on Bitcoin, unlocking escrow services, shared wallets, and corporate custody solutions. Its use of OP_CHECKMULTISIG became the basis for P2SH multi-signature after BIP 16, and multi-sig remains central to Bitcoin security practices.

bips.title: OP_EVAL
bips.summary: Proposes a new OP_EVAL opcode to enable receiver-defined spending conditions via embedded scripts.
bips.summaryMarkdown:
BIP 12 proposes adding an OP_EVAL opcode (redefining OP_NOP1) that allows the receiver of bitcoins to specify the spending conditions rather than the sender. When executed, OP_EVAL deserializes a script from the stack and executes it, enabling transactions where the sender only needs a 20-byte hash of the script.

The proposal was controversial due to the complexity of evaluating data as code. OP_EVAL was ultimately not adopted; it was replaced by the simpler P2SH approach of BIP 16.
bips.impactMarkdown: BIP 12 was a formative proposal in the evolution of Bitcoin scripting. While never adopted, the discussions it generated directly led to the simpler and more secure P2SH approach (BIP 16). The OP_EVAL concept later influenced more advanced scripting proposals.

bips.title: Address Format for pay-to-script-hash
bips.summary: Defines the base58 address format for pay-to-script-hash (P2SH) transactions.
bips.summaryMarkdown:
BIP 13 specifies the address encoding for P2SH transactions. The new address type uses version byte 5 (mainnet) resulting in addresses starting with '3', as opposed to the traditional '1' for pay-to-pubkey-hash addresses. The 20-byte hash represents the hash of a redeem script rather than a public key.

This address format enables sending funds to complex transaction types (multi-signature, time-locked, etc.) using a single address, without the sender needing to understand the underlying script.
bips.impactMarkdown: BIP 13's P2SH address format ('3' addresses) became a fundamental part of Bitcoin's user experience. It enabled multi-signature wallets, improved security for exchanges, and laid the groundwork for SegWit address formats (BIP 49, BIP 84). P2SH addresses remain widely used.

bips.title: Protocol Version and User Agent
bips.summary: Separates the Bitcoin protocol version from the client software version and introduces a user agent string.
bips.summaryMarkdown:
BIP 14 proposes separating the Bitcoin protocol version number from the client implementation version. The version field in the protocol messages becomes the protocol version, while the previously unused sub_version_num field becomes a structured user-agent string (format: /Name:Version/.../) that identifies client software without affecting protocol behavior.

This separation allows different client implementations to interoperate at the same protocol level while allowing network observers to identify client software for statistical purposes.
bips.impactMarkdown: BIP 14's protocol version separation was critical for the diversification of Bitcoin implementations. It allowed alternative clients (BitcoinJ, btcd, libbitcoin) to coexist with Bitcoin Core without version fragmentation, and the user-agent convention remains the standard for network monitoring tools.

bips.title: Aliases
bips.summary: Explores methods for creating human-readable Bitcoin aliases as alternatives to raw addresses.
bips.summaryMarkdown:
BIP 15 surveys several approaches for Bitcoin address aliasing: FirstBits (using the blockchain as an address book), DNS TXT records, server services, and HTTPS web services. It evaluates each on security, usability, and decentralization properties. While not specifying a single standard, the document informed later alias and payment protocol work.

The proposal notes that aliases would be a significant protocol modification requiring careful design, and that getting it right the first time is critical.
bips.impactMarkdown: BIP 15 was not adopted as a standard, but its analysis of alias systems directly informed the development of BIP 70 (Payment Protocol), which BIP 15 itself references as a potential alternative. The discussion around alias usability remains relevant for Bitcoin UX improvements.

bips.title: Pay to Script Hash
bips.summary: Defines the pay-to-script-hash (P2SH) transaction type that shifts spending condition responsibility to the redeemer.
bips.summaryMarkdown:
BIP 16 introduces P2SH as a new standard transaction type using OP_HASH160. A P2SH transaction output locks funds to the hash of a script, and the spender provides both the script and signatures that satisfy it. Validation requires the provided script to hash to the output's hash and the script to execute successfully with the provided signatures.

This was deployed as a soft fork activated on April 1, 2012 (block timestamp >= 1333238400). BIP 16 replaced earlier P2SH proposals (BIP 12's OP_EVAL and BIP 17's OP_CHECKHASHVERIFY).
bips.impactMarkdown: BIP 16 is one of the most impactful soft forks in Bitcoin history. P2SH enabled multi-signature wallets, escrow services, and complex transaction types without protocol-level changes for each use case. It also established the pattern of hashing scripts for addresses, later reused by SegWit (BIP 141) and Taproot (BIP 341).

bips.title: OP_CHECKHASHVERIFY (CHV)
bips.summary: Proposes an alternative P2SH implementation using a new OP_CHECKHASHVERIFY opcode.
bips.summaryMarkdown:
BIP 17 proposes implementing pay-to-script-hash via a new OP_CHECKHASHVERIFY opcode (redefining OP_NOP2). Unlike BIP 16 which uses OP_HASH160 ... OP_EQUAL, CHV hashes the script portion of the scriptSig (after the last OP_CODESEPARATOR) and compares it with a hash provided on the stack.

This was a competing P2SH proposal alongside BIP 16. It was not adopted; BIP 16's simpler approach was implemented instead.
bips.impactMarkdown: BIP 17 was the losing competitor to BIP 16 in the P2SH standardization process. Its approach was more flexible but also more complex. The failure to adopt BIP 17 reinforced the community's preference for simpler, less invasive soft fork designs.

bips.title: hashScriptCheck
bips.summary: Proposes a fundamental redesign of Bitcoin transaction inputs and outputs, replacing scriptSig and scriptPubKey.
bips.summaryMarkdown:
BIP 18 proposes replacing scriptSig and scriptPubKey with three new elements: dataSig (serialized data elements in inputs), scriptCheck (the final element of dataSig, executed with the preceding data preloaded), and hashScriptCheck (replacing scriptPubKey as a hash-based output commitment).

This was a more radical redesign than competing P2SH approaches. It achieved Complete status as a BIP but was not adopted in practice; BIP 16's simpler P2SH won community consensus.
bips.impactMarkdown: BIP 18 represents an alternative design path that was considered during the P2SH standardization. While not adopted, its ideas about separating data from script execution and using hash-based output commitments influenced later thinking about Bitcoin script architecture.

bips.title: M-of-N Standard Transactions (Low SigOp)
bips.summary: Proposes M-of-N multi-signature using OP_CHECKSIG chains instead of OP_CHECKMULTISIG to reduce sigop costs.
bips.summaryMarkdown:
BIP 19 proposes an alternative approach to M-of-N multi-signature that uses chains of OP_CHECKSIG and OP_CHECKSIGVERIFY operations instead of the OP_CHECKMULTISIG opcode. This avoids the 20-sigop-per-transaction penalty that OP_CHECKMULTISIG incurs in the block sigop limit, allowing more multi-signature transactions per block.

Two patterns are defined: N-of-N (all signatures required) using OP_CHECKSIGVERIFY chains, and M-of-N (subset required) using OP_CHECKSIG with OP_SWAP and arithmetic.
bips.impactMarkdown: BIP 19 addressed a practical concern with BIP 11's OP_CHECKMULTISIG approach: the sigop accounting penalty. While BIP 11's approach became the standard for multisig, BIP 19's analysis of sigop costs influenced later improvements to Bitcoin's sigop counting rules.

bips.title: URI Scheme
bips.summary: Proposes a 'bitcoin:' URI scheme for making Bitcoin payments via clickable links and QR codes.
bips.summaryMarkdown:
BIP 20 specifies a URI scheme using the 'bitcoin:' prefix to encode payment requests. The format includes a bitcoin address and optional parameters for amount, label, message, and send instructions. The proposal covers BNF grammar, operating system integration, and transfer amount encoding with decimal and hexadecimal support.

This BIP was replaced by BIP 21, which simplified the URI scheme by removing the version parameter and adopting a cleaner query-string-based format.
bips.impactMarkdown: BIP 20 established the concept of a standardized Bitcoin URI scheme, enabling the 'bitcoin:' link protocol that is now universally supported by wallets. While replaced by BIP 21's simpler design, BIP 20 laid the conceptual groundwork for machine-readable payment requests.

bips.title: URI Scheme
bips.summary: Defines the 'bitcoin:' URI scheme for making payments via clickable links and QR codes.
bips.summaryMarkdown:
BIP 21 specifies the 'bitcoin:' URI scheme for encoding payment requests. It simplifies the earlier BIP 20 design by removing the version parameter and alternative payment amount encoding. The format is `bitcoin:<address>?amount=<value>&label=<text>&message=<text>`. This scheme enables one-click payments from webpages, email links, and QR code scanning.

This BIP replaces BIP 20 and was later superseded by BIP 321.
bips.impactMarkdown: BIP 21 is the universally adopted standard for Bitcoin payment URIs. Every major wallet supports the 'bitcoin:' URI scheme, enabling seamless payment initiation from any application. It was foundational for QR code payments and remains the most widely implemented payment URI standard.

bips.title: getblocktemplate - Fundamentals
bips.summary: Defines the getblocktemplate JSON-RPC method for smart Bitcoin mining.
bips.summaryMarkdown:
BIP 22 specifies the getblocktemplate JSON-RPC method that replaces the older getwork protocol. Instead of sending a simple block header for hashing, the entire block structure is sent to the miner, allowing it to optionally customize and assemble the block. This enables miners to select transactions, add extra data, and optimize their mining strategy.

The template includes the block version, previous block hash, coinbase value, transactions, and target difficulty.
bips.impactMarkdown: BIP 22 revolutionized Bitcoin mining by enabling smart miners to select their own transactions and customize blocks. It became the foundation for modern mining pool protocols and was essential for the development of efficient, decentralized mining infrastructure.

bips.title: getblocktemplate - Pooled Mining
bips.summary: Extends getblocktemplate with pooled mining support including long polling and block proposal.
bips.summaryMarkdown:
BIP 23 extends BIP 22 with features necessary for pooled mining. It introduces long polling support, allowing miners to receive new templates immediately when transactions arrive. It also defines a block proposal mechanism where miners can submit proposed blocks for validation before committing hash power.

Additional features include summary support levels (Level 1, 2, 3) for incremental implementation and enhanced mutation tracking.
bips.impactMarkdown: BIP 23 enabled efficient pooled mining by allowing mining pools to quickly distribute new block templates to miners. Long polling reduced the time miners spent working on outdated templates, improving overall mining efficiency and pool coordination.

bips.title: Duplicate transactions
bips.summary: Fixes a consensus bug where duplicate transactions could cause block chain reorganizations.
bips.summaryMarkdown:
BIP 30 addresses a vulnerability in Bitcoin's consensus rules where duplicate transactions (transactions with the same txid) could cause issues during block chain reorganizations. The proposal adds a consensus rule that a transaction is not valid if a previous transaction with the same txid exists and has any unspent outputs.

This was deployed as a soft fork to prevent potential fork scenarios caused by duplicate coinbase transactions or other duplicate txid situations.
bips.impactMarkdown: BIP 30 closed a subtle but important consensus vulnerability. While the reference implementation was patched, the BIP formalized the rule that duplicate transactions are only valid if the earlier one has no spendable outputs remaining, providing a clear specification for all implementations.

bips.title: Pong message
bips.summary: Adds a pong message to the Bitcoin protocol for detecting dead peer connections.
bips.summaryMarkdown:
BIP 31 adds a 'pong' message to the Bitcoin peer-to-peer protocol. When a peer sends a 'ping' message with a random nonce, the receiving peer responds with a 'pong' containing the same nonce. This allows clients to detect dead connections (e.g., after sleep/wake cycles on mobile devices), measure latency, and identify overloaded peers.

The protocol version was bumped to 60002 to support this feature.
bips.impactMarkdown: BIP 31's ping/pong mechanism became essential for mobile Bitcoin wallets and laptops that frequently suspend. It improved network reliability by enabling timely detection of stale connections and provided a standardized latency measurement tool for peer selection algorithms.

bips.title: Hierarchical Deterministic Wallets
bips.summary: Defines hierarchical deterministic (HD) wallets for generating a tree of keypairs from a single seed.
bips.summaryMarkdown:
BIP 32 specifies the standard for hierarchical deterministic wallets (HD wallets). It enables deriving a tree of keypairs from a single master seed, allowing selective sharing of public keys without exposing private keys. The specification covers master key generation, child key derivation (normal and hardened), and serialization formats for extended public/private keys (xpub/xprv).

HD wallets eliminate the need for frequent backups, enable deterministic address generation, and allow webshops to generate receive addresses without access to private keys.
bips.impactMarkdown: BIP 32 is one of the most impactful standards in cryptocurrency. It made wallet backups a one-time operation, enabled hierarchical account structures (BIP 44), and became the foundation for virtually all modern cryptocurrency wallets. Its xpub/xprv key format is universal across the industry.

bips.title: Stratized Nodes
bips.summary: Proposes specialized blockchain service nodes to offload validation from lightweight clients.
bips.summaryMarkdown:
BIP 33 introduces the concept of 'stratized nodes' — specialized Bitcoin nodes that provide blockchain data services to lightweight clients. It defines two new service flags: NODE_SERVICE (for nodes that respond to getoutputs/getspends queries) and NODE_STRATIZED (for nodes providing full validation services). This proposal aimed to address blockchain scalability for portable and low-end devices.

The proposal was an early attempt at solving the lightweight client problem before BIP 37 (Bloom filtering) became the standard approach.
bips.impactMarkdown: BIP 33 was not adopted as a standard, as BIP 37's Bloom filter approach provided a simpler and more privacy-preserving solution for lightweight clients. However, the concept of specialized service nodes influenced later infrastructure developments like Electrum servers and Bitcoin Core's simplified payment verification.

bips.title: Block v2, Height in Coinbase
bips.summary: Introduces block version 2 and requires the block height to be included in the coinbase transaction.
bips.summaryMarkdown:
BIP 34 introduces block version 2 and requires miners to include the block height as the first element in the coinbase transaction's scriptSig. This change enforces block and transaction uniqueness, assists unconnected block validation, and provides a clear upgrade path for versioned blocks.

Activation followed a two-phase process: a 75% threshold (750 of last 1000 blocks version 2+) for rejecting invalid v2 blocks, followed by a 95% threshold for rejecting all version 1 blocks.
bips.impactMarkdown: BIP 34 was the first soft fork to use miner signalling for activation, establishing the pattern that would be refined by BIP 9. It also solved the duplicate coinbase transaction problem and made block height universally accessible from the coinbase, simplifying block validation for all implementations.

bips.title: mempool message
bips.summary: Adds a mempool message to expose a node's transaction memory pool to the network.
bips.summaryMarkdown:
BIP 35 adds a 'mempool' message to the Bitcoin protocol, allowing peers to request the contents of a node's unconfirmed transaction memory pool. Nodes respond with an 'inv' message listing all MSG_TX hashes in their mempool. This enables SPV clients to discover zero-confirmation transactions, miners to recover transactions after restart, and remote network diagnostics.

The feature is enabled when a node advertises protocol version >= 60002 and has the NODE_NETWORK service bit set.
bips.impactMarkdown: BIP 35 became essential for various network operations. Miners use it to repopulate their mempool after restarts, ensuring they don't miss fee-paying transactions. SPV clients benefit from discovering relevant unconfirmed transactions. It also enabled network monitoring tools to analyze mempool statistics.

bips.title: Custom Services
bips.summary: Adds extensible service fields to the version message for announcing custom protocol extensions.
bips.summaryMarkdown:
BIP 36 proposes adding new fields to the 'version' message — service_count and service_list — allowing nodes to announce custom services without polluting the limited 64-bit services field. It provides a framework for protocol extensions like DHT, distributed pools, lightweight client support, and custom transports.

The goal was to encourage experimentation with custom services while avoiding collisions between different protocol extensions.
bips.impactMarkdown: BIP 36 was not widely adopted. The Bitcoin ecosystem instead favored simpler approaches like dedicated service bits for major features and out-of-protocol negotiation for custom services. However, it represented an early attempt to formalize protocol extensibility.

bips.title: Connection Bloom filtering
bips.summary: Adds Bloom filter-based transaction filtering for SPV clients to reduce bandwidth usage.
bips.summaryMarkdown:
BIP 37 introduces connection-level Bloom filtering to the Bitcoin peer-to-peer protocol. SPV clients can set a Bloom filter on each connection after the version handshake, and peers will only send transactions matching the filter. The probabilistic nature of Bloom filters provides tunable privacy (false positive rate chosen by the client) while reducing bandwidth.

Three new messages are added: filterload (set filter), filteradd (add data to filter), and filterclear (remove filter). This was the primary mechanism for SPV wallet synchronization for years.
bips.impactMarkdown: BIP 37 was transformative for mobile Bitcoin wallets, reducing bandwidth usage by orders of magnitude. It enabled the 'Bitcoin Wallet' Android app and similar SPV clients to synchronize quickly on metered connections. However, privacy concerns later led to its deprecation in favor of BIP 157/158 (compact block filters).

bips.title: Passphrase-protected private key
bips.summary: Standardizes encryption of private keys with a passphrase for paper wallets and physical bitcoins.
bips.summaryMarkdown:
BIP 38 specifies a method for encrypting Bitcoin private keys with a passphrase, producing a 58-character Base58Check-encoded string that can be printed on paper wallets or physical bitcoins. The encryption uses scrypt key derivation with salting to resist brute-force attacks.

Two encoding schemes are defined: one for encrypting any known private key, and another for shared creation where the manufacturer never learns the full passphrase. The format includes a 32-bit address hash for correlation without decryption.
bips.impactMarkdown: BIP 38 enabled a new category of two-factor paper wallets and physical bitcoins. Users could store encrypted keys publicly while keeping only a passphrase secret. It found significant use in physical Bitcoin products, paper wallet generators, and offline storage solutions, though its complexity limited mainstream adoption.

bips.title: Mnemonic code for generating deterministic keys
bips.summary: Defines a mnemonic word phrase for human-friendly backup of deterministic wallet seeds.
bips.summaryMarkdown:
BIP 39 specifies the standard for generating mnemonic sentences (typically 12 or 24 words) from a random seed, which can then be used to generate deterministic wallets via BIP 32 or similar methods. A wordlist of 2048 carefully chosen words is provided, with support for multiple languages.

The process has two parts: generating the mnemonic from entropy (with optional passphrase), and converting it to a binary seed using PBKDF2 with 2048 hash rounds.
bips.impactMarkdown: BIP 39 is arguably the most user-facing improvement in cryptocurrency wallet technology. The 12/24-word mnemonic phrase is now the universal standard for wallet backup across thousands of applications. It replaced error-prone hex backups with human-readable phrases that can be written on paper or memorized.

bips.title: A finite monetary supply for Bitcoin
bips.summary: An April Fools' BIP humorously addressing the 'problem' of Bitcoin's supposedly infinite monetary supply.
bips.summaryMarkdown:
BIP 42 is an April Fools' Day BIP that humorously addresses the 'issue' that Bitcoin's subsidy calculation uses C++ undefined behavior — specifically, shifting a 64-bit integer beyond its size, which in C++ is undefined behavior. On most platforms this results in the subsidy cycling through zero forever rather than staying at zero.

The BIP 'proposes' to fix this to ensure Bitcoin's monetary supply is finite, playing on the irony that Bitcoin's actual code would eventually create infinite coins due to the undefined behavior, while everyone believes supply is capped at 21 million.
bips.impactMarkdown: BIP 42 is one of Bitcoin's most famous humor BIPs. It highlights the difference between Bitcoin's intended monetary policy (21 million cap) and what the code technically does (eventually cycles back to nonzero subsidies due to undefined behavior in C++). It serves as a reminder that even well-audited code can have subtle issues.

bips.title: Purpose Field for Deterministic Wallets
bips.summary: Introduces a purpose field in HD wallet derivation paths to enable multiple wallet standards.
bips.summaryMarkdown:
BIP 43 introduces a 'purpose' field as the first level of the BIP 32 derivation path (`m / purpose' / *`). This allows different wallet standards to have dedicated, non-overlapping derivation paths. The purpose number typically matches the BIP number, ensuring unique paths for each standard.

This simple addition solved the interoperability problem where different wallets using BIP 32 would produce incompatible address structures.
bips.impactMarkdown: BIP 43 was essential for wallet standardization. It enabled multiple derivation standards (BIP 44 for multi-account, BIP 49 for SegWit, BIP 84 for native SegWit, BIP 86 for Taproot) to coexist without conflict. Without it, wallet interoperability would be far more fragmented.

bips.title: Multi-Account Hierarchy for Deterministic Wallets
bips.summary: Defines a multi-account hierarchy for HD wallets with support for multiple coins and accounts.
bips.summaryMarkdown:
BIP 44 builds on BIP 32 and BIP 43 to define a comprehensive 5-level derivation path: `m / purpose' / coin_type' / account' / change / address_index`. This structure supports multiple cryptocurrencies (via coin_type), multiple accounts per user, internal/external chains for each account, and millions of addresses per chain.

This is a particular application of BIP 43 with purpose value 44'. It requires BIP 32 for key derivation and BIP 43 for the purpose field.
bips.impactMarkdown: BIP 44 became the de facto standard for HD wallet structure across the entire cryptocurrency industry. Almost every hardware wallet, software wallet, and exchange uses BIP 44 derivation paths. It enabled interoperable wallets where users can restore their entire wallet structure from a single seed phrase.

bips.title: Structure for Deterministic P2SH Multisignature Wallets
bips.summary: Defines a derivation structure for hierarchical deterministic multi-party multi-signature wallets.
bips.summaryMarkdown:
BIP 45 defines a derivation structure for HD P2SH multi-party multi-signature (HDPM) wallets based on BIP 32 and BIP 43. It uses the path `m / purpose' / cosigner_index / change / address_index`, where `purpose` is 45'. Multiple parties each generate master keys independently, then derive shared multisig addresses without communication.

The standard supports m-of-n wallets where address generation requires no interaction between parties, but transaction creation and signing requires communication.
bips.impactMarkdown: BIP 45 enabled standardized multi-signature wallets where multiple parties could generate addresses independently. It was used by BitPay and other multi-sig services, though its adoption was limited compared to BIP 44's single-signature standard.

bips.title: Address Scheme for Timelocked Fidelity Bonds
bips.summary: Defines HD wallet derivation for timelocked addresses used in fidelity bonds to resist Sybil attacks.
bips.summaryMarkdown:
BIP 46 defines a derivation scheme for HD wallets that create timelocked addresses using OP_CHECKLOCKTIMEVERIFY for fidelity bonds. The path follows the pattern of BIP 49/84/86 for ease of implementation. Fidelity bonds resist Sybil attacks in decentralized protocols by requiring value to be locked up, sacrificing the time-value of money.

Users can back up all their fidelity bonds by storing only the HD seed and a reference to this BIP, without needing to backup individual timelock values.
bips.impactMarkdown: BIP 46 enables a novel privacy and security mechanism. Fidelity bonds created with this standard allow decentralized protocols like JoinMarket to resist Sybil attacks while keeping private keys in cold storage. The deterministic derivation ensures recoverability without individual bond backups.

bips.title: Reusable Payment Codes for Hierarchical Deterministic Wallets
bips.summary: Defines reusable payment codes that enable private, non-reusable Bitcoin payments without address reuse.
bips.summaryMarkdown:
BIP 47 introduces reusable payment codes — publicly shareable codes that allow senders to generate unique, non-reusable Bitcoin addresses for each payment without requiring the receiver to be online. Each payment uses a different derived address, preventing address reuse privacy leaks while maintaining a single public identifier.

Payment codes provide privacy benefits similar to stealth addresses but work with SPV clients and don't require blockchain storage for notification transactions.
bips.impactMarkdown: BIP 47 addresses a fundamental privacy problem: the tension between advertising a single payment identifier and avoiding address reuse. It enables merchants to publish one code while customers generate unique addresses per transaction. Though conceptually influential, adoption was limited by complexity and the rise of Lightning Network.

bips.title: Multi-Script Hierarchy for Multi-Sig Wallets
bips.summary: Defines a derivation path for deterministic multi-signature wallets supporting multiple script types.
bips.summaryMarkdown:
BIP 48 defines a logical hierarchy for deterministic multi-sig wallets using the derivation path `m/48'`. It extends BIP 43 and BIP 44 to support multiple script types (P2SH, P2WSH, etc.) within a single multi-sig framework, and formalizes the existing industry practice of using `m/48'` paths.

This BIP allows future script types to be added without requiring a new BIP for each one, and supports multiple accounts, chains, and address indices.
bips.impactMarkdown: BIP 48 standardized the `m/48'` derivation path already in use by several multi-sig wallet implementations. By supporting multiple script types, it provided forward compatibility for new address formats while maintaining interoperability between existing wallets.

bips.title: Derivation scheme for P2WPKH-nested-in-P2SH based accounts
bips.summary: Defines HD wallet derivation for SegWit addresses nested in P2SH (compatible SegWit).
bips.summaryMarkdown:
BIP 49 defines the derivation scheme for HD wallets using P2WPKH-nested-in-P2SH (SegWit addresses backward-compatible with older wallets). The derivation path is `m/49'/coin_type'/account'/change/address_index`. This was the standard for SegWit wallets before native SegWit (BIP 84) became widely supported.

Using dedicated accounts for SegWit ensures that non-BIP 49 wallets either see the full account or nothing at all, preventing silent missing-UTXO issues.
bips.impactMarkdown: BIP 49 was crucial during the SegWit transition period. It enabled backward-compatible SegWit addresses (starting with '3') that worked with older wallets while already benefiting from SegWit's transaction malleability fix and lower fees. It was the most widely used SegWit standard until native SegWit (bech32) gained universal support.

bips.title: March 2013 Chain Fork Post-Mortem
bips.summary: Documents the March 2013 chain fork incident and its root cause in Berkeley DB lock configuration.
bips.summaryMarkdown:
BIP 50 is a post-mortem analysis of the March 11-12, 2013 chain fork, one of Bitcoin's most significant network incidents. A block with an unusually large number of transaction inputs was mined, which Bitcoin 0.8 nodes could process but pre-0.8 nodes (using Berkeley DB with insufficient lock limits) rejected, causing a chain split.

The fork was resolved when major mining pools (BTCGuild and Slush) downgraded to Bitcoin 0.7 to place majority hashpower on the pre-0.8 chain. A double-spend was successfully executed during the incident, though it was experimental rather than malicious.
bips.impactMarkdown: BIP 50 documents Bitcoin's first major chain fork incident. The post-mortem led to critical improvements: the switch from BDB to LevelDB, better testing of edge-case blocks, and development of emergency response procedures. It remains a key reference for understanding consensus safety in decentralized systems.

bips.title: Durable, Low Energy Bitcoin PoW
bips.summary: Proposes optical proof-of-work (oPoW) to decouple Bitcoin mining from energy consumption.
bips.summaryMarkdown:
BIP 52 proposes replacing Bitcoin's Hashcash proof-of-work with optical proof-of-work (oPoW), designed to be most efficiently computed using photonic processors. The goal is to shift mining operating expenses from electricity (OPEX) to hardware (CAPEX), making mining feasible outside of low-electricity-cost regions and reducing Bitcoin's environmental impact.

This would require a hard fork and would significantly change Bitcoin's mining economics. The proposal remains in Draft status.
bips.impactMarkdown: BIP 52 addresses Bitcoin's energy consumption criticism but proposes a fundamental change to the security model. As a hard fork requiring near-universal consensus and introducing a completely new PoW algorithm, it has not advanced beyond Draft status. It remains a reference point for discussions about alternative PoW designs.

bips.title: Disallow 64-byte transactions
bips.summary: Proposes disallowing 64-byte transactions to fix Merkle tree weaknesses and block malleability.
bips.summaryMarkdown:
BIP 53 proposes disallowing Bitcoin transactions serialized to exactly 64 bytes (without witness). Transactions of this size have the same serialized length as two concatenated SHA256 hashes, which can be exploited to create fake Merkle proof attacks against light clients and introduce block malleability.

The 64-byte minimum was already enforced by Bitcoin Core's relay policy since 2018 (minimum 65 bytes), and this BIP proposes making it a consensus rule.
bips.impactMarkdown: BIP 53 addresses a real cryptographic weakness in Bitcoin's Merkle tree construction. The block malleability and light client attack vectors are well-understood, but making this a consensus rule rather than just relay policy requires careful consideration. It represents ongoing efforts to harden Bitcoin's security model.

bips.title: Consensus Cleanup
bips.summary: BIP 54: Consensus Cleanup.
bips.summaryMarkdown: Draft generated from official BIP metadata. Requires technical review before editorial publication.
bips.impactMarkdown: Impact to be verified during maintainer review.

bips.title: Fixed Length "version" Message (Relay-Transactions Field)
bips.summary: Proposes making the version message fixed-length by integrating the relay transactions flag into the protocol.
bips.summaryMarkdown:
BIP 60 addresses an inconsistency introduced by BIP 37, which added an optional RelayTransactions field to the version message. This broke the fixed-length property of Bitcoin protocol messages. BIP 60 proposes integrating this flag into the protocol itself, restoring fixed-length message semantics for simpler deserialization and validation.

The proposal was motivated by concerns that optional fields make message format checking harder and complicate parser implementations.
bips.impactMarkdown: BIP 60 was not adopted; the Bitcoin protocol continued to use variable-length version messages. The RelayTransactions field from BIP 37 remained as an optional extension. This BIP represents a viewpoint favoring strict message format discipline that was not shared by the broader development community.

bips.title: Reject P2P message
bips.summary: Adds a Reject P2P message type allowing nodes to report why a transaction or block was rejected.
bips.summaryMarkdown:
BIP 61 introduces a new `reject` message type for the Bitcoin peer-to-peer network. When a node rejects a transaction, block, or bans a peer for protocol violations, it can send a reject message containing the reason. The message includes the type of item rejected (tx or block), a rejection code, and an optional human-readable explanation string.

This mechanism improves interoperability between different Bitcoin implementations by providing feedback when peers send invalid data. It also gives SPV clients a hint when their transactions are rejected due to insufficient fees or priority, helping users understand why a transaction is not propagating.
bips.impactMarkdown: Deployed in Bitcoin Core 0.9.0 and widely adopted, the reject message became a standard debugging tool for developers and node operators. While the message format is straightforward, its main impact has been operational: node operators can diagnose connectivity issues and protocol violations more easily. The BIP itself was later partially reverted in Bitcoin Core 0.20.0 due to privacy concerns, as the reject messages could leak information about which transactions a node considers valid.

bips.title: Dealing with malleability
bips.summary: Specifies changes to transaction validity rules to eliminate transaction malleability, making it impossible to modify a transaction in flight without access to private keys.
bips.summaryMarkdown:
BIP 62 proposes a set of consensus rule changes to address transaction malleability, a property that allows a valid transaction to be modified in transit without invalidating it. The proposal targets multiple sources of malleability: ECDSA signature encoding, scriptSigs, and the serialization format. The BIP specifies strict DER encoding for signatures, limits on the number of signature checking operations, and rules for the scriptSig format.

The BIP was closed without full deployment as its proposals were superseded by Segregated Witness (BIP 141), which solves malleability more comprehensively by moving the signature data outside the transaction ID. Individual elements of BIP 62, particularly the strict DER encoding requirement, were deployed separately in BIP 66.
bips.impactMarkdown: Although BIP 62 was never adopted as a complete package, its analysis of malleability sources informed later solutions. The strict DER encoding requirement became BIP 66 and was deployed as a soft fork. The broader malleability problem was ultimately solved by SegWit (BIP 141), which removes signature data from the transaction hash. BIP 62 remains historically important as the first systematic attempt to classify and fix transaction malleability.

bips.title: getutxo message
bips.summary: Defines a getutxo P2P message that allows lightweight clients to query the unspent transaction output set from full nodes.
bips.summaryMarkdown:
BIP 64 specifies a new `getutxo` message type for the Bitcoin P2P protocol. The message enables a peer to request UTXO (unspent transaction output) lookups from a full node by providing a set of outpoints (transaction hash + output index). The responding node returns the corresponding UTXO entries including their scriptPubKey and confirmation status.

The primary motivation was to support lightweight applications such as assurance contracts, where an SPV client needs to quickly verify whether a pledge has been revoked via double-spend.
bips.impactMarkdown: The getutxo message was implemented in Bitcoin Core but never became widely used on the network. The BIP was eventually closed as the approach was superseded by more comprehensive solutions for lightweight client support, such as client-side filtering (BIP 157/158).

bips.title: OP_CHECKLOCKTIMEVERIFY
bips.summary: Introduces OP_CHECKLOCKTIMEVERIFY, a new opcode that enables transaction outputs to be made unspendable until a specified future time or block height.
bips.summaryMarkdown:
BIP 65 adds OP_CHECKLOCKTIMEVERIFY (CLTV) to Bitcoin’s scripting system. The opcode redefines the existing NOP2 opcode and allows a script to enforce that a transaction output cannot be spent until a specified absolute locktime — either a block height or a UNIX timestamp. When executed, CLTV checks that the top stack item is less than or equal to the transaction’s nLockTime field, ensuring the output remains locked until the required time.

CLTV enables time-locked transactions directly in script, without requiring multi-party cooperation. This was a critical building block for payment channels, escrow arrangements, and other smart contract applications. Together with CSV (BIP 112), CLTV forms the basis for off-chain payment channels and the Lightning Network.
bips.impactMarkdown: CLTV was activated as a soft fork in December 2015 and is one of the most significant opcode additions to Bitcoin Script. It enabled a new class of time-sensitive smart contracts. The activation used BIP 9 version bits with a 95% miner threshold.

bips.title: Strict DER signatures
bips.summary: Restricts ECDSA signatures in Bitcoin transactions to strict DER encoding, removing reliance on OpenSSL for consensus-critical signature parsing.
bips.summaryMarkdown:
BIP 66 mandates that all ECDSA signatures used in Bitcoin transactions must follow strict Distinguished Encoding Rules (DER) encoding. Previously, Bitcoin relied on OpenSSL for signature validation, which accepted various deviations from the DER standard. When OpenSSL changes in versions 1.0.0p and 1.0.1k tightened DER enforcement, nodes could diverge on which transactions were valid — a consensus failure risk.

By codifying strict DER encoding as a consensus rule, BIP 66 removed Bitcoin’s dependency on OpenSSL’s signature parsing behavior. The BIP specifies exact byte sequences for signatures passed to OP_CHECKSIG, OP_CHECKSIGVERIFY, OP_CHECKMULTISIG, and OP_CHECKMULTISIGVERIFY.
bips.impactMarkdown: Activated as a soft fork in July 2015, BIP 66 was one of the early applications of BIP 9 version-bit activation. It successfully eliminated a source of consensus fragility by standardizing signature encoding at the protocol level.

bips.title: Deterministic Pay-to-script-hash multi-signature addresses through public key sorting
bips.summary: Defines deterministic ordering and encoding of public keys for P2SH multisignature addresses, ensuring the same set of keys always produces the same address.
bips.summaryMarkdown:
BIP 67 standardizes how public keys are sorted and encoded when creating pay-to-script-hash (P2SH) multisignature addresses. Without ordering rules, a set of n public keys with m required signatures could produce up to 2(n!) different P2SH addresses, each with a different redeem script. BIP 67 mandates lexicographic sorting of public keys by their binary encoding before hashing.

This determinism is particularly important for HD wallets using multisignature schemes. Participants can share only their master public keys and the required signature count, and all wallets will independently derive the same addresses.
bips.impactMarkdown: BIP 67 was widely adopted by wallet implementations following its publication. While not a consensus change, it became a de facto standard for multisignature address generation, improving interoperability between different wallet software.

bips.title: Relative lock-time using consensus-enforced sequence numbers
bips.summary: Repurposes the sequence number field to enforce relative lock-time, enabling a transaction input to remain invalid for a defined period after its output is confirmed.
bips.summaryMarkdown:
BIP 68 introduces relative lock-time (RLT) to Bitcoin by giving consensus-enforced meaning to the sequence number field. Previously, sequence numbers were intended for transaction replacement but were never properly implemented. BIP 68 redefines them so that an input cannot be spent until a specified number of blocks or amount of time has elapsed since the referenced output was confirmed.

The relative lock-time can express either a number of blocks or a multiple of 512 seconds. The BIP applies when the transaction version is 2 or higher and bit 31 of the sequence number is not set.
bips.impactMarkdown: Activated as part of the 2016 soft fork package alongside BIP 9, BIP 112 (CSV), and BIP 113, BIP 68 is fundamental to off-chain payment channels. Relative lock-time enables HTLC timeouts in the Lightning Network, transforming the sequence number field from a legacy unused feature into a critical smart contract primitive.

bips.title: Lexicographical Indexing of Transaction Inputs and Outputs
bips.summary: Standardizes lexicographic ordering of transaction inputs and outputs to eliminate wallet fingerprinting and improve privacy.
bips.summaryMarkdown:
BIP 69 addresses the privacy problem of wallet fingerprinting through transaction input and output ordering. Without a standard ordering convention, each wallet client tends to order inputs and outputs in a unique way, creating observable patterns on the blockchain that can identify which software created a given transaction.

BIP 69 specifies that inputs should be sorted lexicographically by the hash of the referenced previous transaction, while outputs should be sorted by value. This deterministic ordering prevents fingerprinting while remaining easy to audit.
bips.impactMarkdown: BIP 69 is an informational standard rather than a consensus rule. While some wallets adopted it, compliance has been inconsistent. The BIP highlights the privacy implications of implementation-specific behavior and provides a concrete standard for wallets to converge on.

bips.title: Payment Protocol
bips.summary: Defines a payment protocol enabling encrypted communication between merchant and customer for secure Bitcoin payment requests.
bips.summaryMarkdown:
BIP 70 introduces a payment protocol that replaces the simple bitcoin: URI scheme with a richer request-response interaction. When a customer initiates a payment, the merchant’s server returns a digitally signed PaymentRequest containing the merchant’s identity, payment details, and refund address. The customer’s wallet validates the signature, presents the payment information, and submits the signed transaction back as a Payment message. The merchant can then reply with a PaymentACK confirming receipt.

This protocol solves several problems with the basic URI approach: it prevents man-in-the-middle attacks by authenticating the payment request, provides a refund address automatically, and allows the merchant to update payment details dynamically. X.509 certificates provide identity verification.
bips.impactMarkdown: BIP 70 was deployed in several major wallets including Bitcoin Core and was used by payment processors such as BitPay. However, adoption was limited by the complexity of certificate management and was eventually removed from Bitcoin Core 0.20.0 due to low usage. Despite limited deployment, BIP 70 influenced later payment protocol designs.

bips.title: Payment Protocol MIME types
bips.summary: Defines MIME media types for the BIP 70 Payment Protocol messages.
bips.summaryMarkdown: BIP 71 specifies three MIME media types for the Payment Protocol defined in BIP 70: `application/bitcoin-paymentrequest` for PaymentRequest messages, `application/bitcoin-payment` for Payment messages, and `application/bitcoin-paymentack` for PaymentACK messages. These types allow HTTP-based transport of payment protocol messages using standard Content-Type and Accept headers.
bips.impactMarkdown: BIP 71 is a supporting standard for BIP 70, deployed wherever BIP 70 was implemented. The MIME types are registered with IANA.

bips.title: bitcoin: uri extensions for Payment Protocol
bips.summary: Extends the bitcoin: URI scheme to support the BIP 70 Payment Protocol by adding an r parameter for payment request URLs.
bips.summaryMarkdown: BIP 72 extends BIP 21’s bitcoin: URI scheme with a new `r` parameter that contains the URL of a BIP 70 PaymentRequest. When a wallet processes a URI with the `r` parameter, it fetches the payment request from the specified URL and follows the BIP 70 protocol. If the wallet does not support BIP 70, it can fall back to the basic address.
bips.impactMarkdown: BIP 72 was implemented alongside BIP 70 and shared its adoption trajectory. The `r` parameter convention is still recognized by some wallets as a fallback mechanism.

bips.title: Use "Accept" header for response type negotiation with Payment Request URLs
bips.summary: Uses HTTP Accept headers for content negotiation of payment protocol messages, eliminating different URLs for different formats.
bips.summaryMarkdown:
BIP 73 simplifies the BIP 70 payment protocol by using the HTTP `Accept` header to negotiate the response format, rather than requiring different URL paths for different MIME types. The server returns the appropriate content type based on what the wallet supports.

This approach reduces URL complexity and aligns with standard HTTP content negotiation practices.
bips.impactMarkdown: BIP 73 was a minor refinement to the BIP 70 protocol stack, implemented in supporting wallets and servers but with limited long-term adoption.

bips.title: Allow zero value OP_RETURN in Payment Protocol
bips.summary: Extends BIP 70 Payment Protocol to allow zero-value OP_RETURN outputs in PaymentRequest messages for data carrier applications.
bips.summaryMarkdown:
BIP 74 modifies the BIP 70 Payment Protocol to permit OP_RETURN outputs with a value of zero in PaymentRequest messages. The original BIP 70 specification allowed only outputs with non-zero values, which prevented using the payment protocol for applications that embed data in transactions via OP_RETURN.

This extension was requested for use cases such as notarization and colored coins.
bips.impactMarkdown: BIP 74 was closed as the Payment Protocol ecosystem declined. The use of OP_RETURN evolved independently through other mechanisms.

bips.title: Out of Band Address Exchange using Payment Protocol Encryption
bips.summary: Extends BIP 70 with out-of-band address exchange using encrypted Payment Protocol messages for enhanced privacy.
bips.summaryMarkdown: BIP 75 provides two enhancements to BIP 70: out-of-band address exchange and encrypted Payment Protocol messages. The first allows parties to exchange Bitcoin addresses through the Payment Protocol without requiring a separate communication channel. The second encrypts the PaymentRequest and Payment messages so that only the intended recipient can read them.
bips.impactMarkdown: BIP 75 was implemented by some payment processors but shared the overall limited adoption trajectory of BIP 70.

bips.title: Async Payjoin
bips.summary: BIP 77: Async Payjoin.
bips.summaryMarkdown: Draft generated from official BIP metadata. Requires technical review before editorial publication.
bips.impactMarkdown: Impact to be verified during maintainer review.

bips.title: A Simple Payjoin Proposal
bips.summary: Proposes a simple payjoin protocol allowing the receiver to contribute an input to their own payment, improving privacy for both parties.
bips.summaryMarkdown: BIP 78 specifies the Payjoin protocol (P2EP), where the recipient of a payment contributes an input to the transaction. This breaks the common-input-ownership heuristic that blockchain analysts use to cluster addresses. The sender creates a provisional transaction, the receiver adds their input and a change output, and the sender signs and broadcasts the result.
bips.impactMarkdown: BIP 78 was deployed in several wallets including Wasabi Wallet and Bitcoin Core. Payjoin remains one of the most practical privacy techniques for Bitcoin transactions.

bips.title: Bustapay :: a practical coinjoin protocol
bips.summary: Describes Bustapay, a practical coinjoin protocol allowing multiple senders to combine payments into a single transaction.
bips.summaryMarkdown: BIP 79 specifies Bustapay, a coinjoin protocol designed for practical, low-overhead transaction merging. Unlike Chaumian CoinJoin implementations requiring specialized infrastructure, Bustapay aims to be simple enough for integration into wallet software without external coordination servers.
bips.impactMarkdown: BIP 79 was closed as its approach was superseded by more sophisticated coinjoin implementations like Chaumian CoinJoin used in Wasabi Wallet.

bips.title: Hierarchy for Non-Colored Voting Pool Deterministic Multisig Wallets
bips.summary: Defines a BIP 32 hierarchy for non-colored voting pool deterministic multisignature wallets.
bips.summaryMarkdown:
BIP 80 specifies a logical hierarchy for deterministic wallets used in non-colored voting pools based on BIP 32. It defines key derivation paths for managing multiple participants, voting rights, and fund distribution within a pool structure.

The BIP targets governance applications like decentralized decision-making pools rather than simple payment scenarios.
bips.impactMarkdown: BIP 80 was closed and did not see significant adoption. The concept of voting pool hierarchies on Bitcoin did not gain traction.

bips.title: Hierarchy for Colored Voting Pool Deterministic Multisig Wallets
bips.summary: Defines a BIP 32 hierarchy for colored voting pool deterministic multisignature wallets.
bips.summaryMarkdown:
BIP 81 specifies a logical hierarchy for colored coin voting pool deterministic wallets based on BIP 32, extending concepts from BIP 80. It defines key derivation paths for managing colored assets within a voting pool structure.

The BIP was part of a broader effort to enable complex financial instruments on Bitcoin using colored coins.
bips.impactMarkdown: Like BIP 80, BIP 81 was closed without significant adoption. The colored coins approach was largely superseded by tokens on other platforms.

bips.title: Dynamic Hierarchical Deterministic Key Trees
bips.summary: Defines a dynamic hierarchical deterministic key tree scheme for on-demand creation of key derivation branches.
bips.summaryMarkdown:
BIP 83 proposes a scheme for dynamic key derivation that extends BIP 32. Unlike BIP 32’s static hierarchy, dynamic key trees allow new branches to be created on demand without predefining the entire structure.

The scheme defines how wallets can generate new derivation paths as needed, using the master seed to derive branch-specific keys.
bips.impactMarkdown: BIP 83 was closed and did not see adoption. The standard BIP 32 / BIP 43 / BIP 44 hierarchy proved sufficient for most wallet use cases.

bips.title: Derivation scheme for P2WPKH based accounts
bips.summary: Defines the derivation scheme for native SegWit P2WPKH bech32 addresses on BIP 32 HD wallets.
bips.summaryMarkdown:
BIP 84 specifies the key derivation path `m/84’/0’/0’` for native SegWit P2WPKH addresses using bech32 (BIP 173). This is analogous to BIP 44 for legacy (`m/44’/0’/0’`) and BIP 49 for nested SegWit (`m/49’/0’/0’`), using purpose code 84 for native SegWit.

The BIP ensures deterministic wallets generate the same set of native SegWit addresses from a given seed, providing interoperability between implementations. Native SegWit addresses offer lower fees and smaller block space usage.
bips.impactMarkdown: BIP 84 is widely adopted as the standard derivation path for modern Bitcoin wallets. Most wallets created since 2019 default to BIP 84 for new SegWit wallets, representing current best practice.

bips.title: Deterministic Entropy From BIP32 Keychains
bips.summary: Defines a method to generate deterministic entropy from BIP 32 keychains, allowing a single seed to produce keys for multiple cryptocurrencies.
bips.summaryMarkdown:
BIP 85 specifies a technique for using a BIP 32 seed to derive entropy for other deterministic wallets or cryptographic applications. Using the derivation path `m/83699’/0’/0’`, a master seed can generate child seeds for different cryptocurrencies or wallet standards.

The motivation is the “one seed to rule them all” concept — managing a single master seed instead of separate seeds for each application.
bips.impactMarkdown: BIP 85 has been adopted by several multi-currency wallets and is considered a best practice for cross-chain seed management, reducing the attack surface of seed storage.

bips.title: Key Derivation for Single Key P2TR Outputs
bips.summary: Defines the key derivation scheme for single-key P2TR Taproot outputs using BIP 32 HD wallets.
bips.summaryMarkdown:
BIP 86 specifies the derivation path `m/86’/0’/0’` for single-key Pay-to-Taproot (P2TR) addresses following BIP 341. This continues the pattern from BIP 44 (legacy), BIP 49 (nested SegWit), and BIP 84 (native SegWit), using purpose code 86 for Taproot.

Taproot outputs (activated November 2021) offer improved privacy, lower fees, and greater scripting flexibility.
bips.impactMarkdown: BIP 86 is the current standard derivation path for new Bitcoin wallets using Taproot, completing the HD wallet evolution from legacy (44) through SegWit (84) to Taproot (86).

bips.title: Hierarchy for Deterministic Multisig Wallets
bips.summary: Defines a BIP 32 hierarchy for deterministic multisignature wallets, providing a standard for shared-account address derivation.
bips.summaryMarkdown:
BIP 87 specifies the derivation path `m/87’/0’/0’` for multisignature wallets using BIP 32. Unlike the m/45’ path from BIP 45, BIP 87 adds a purpose code (87’) and deeper hierarchy to support multiple multisig accounts from a single seed.

The BIP addresses the need for a standard multisig derivation scheme enabling recovery from seed phrases alone, extending the BIP 44 pattern into multisig territory.
bips.impactMarkdown: BIP 87 has been adopted by multisig-specialized wallets including Casa and Specter, providing a foundation for interoperable multisig wallet recovery.

bips.title: Hierarchical Deterministic Path Templates
bips.summary: Defines a template format for expressing constraints on hierarchical deterministic wallet paths.
bips.summaryMarkdown:
BIP 88 specifies a notation for HD path templates describing the structure and constraints of BIP 32 derivation paths. Templates indicate which account numbers, chain types, and address indices are valid.

This standard allows wallet developers to describe supported derivation patterns without hardcoding specific path formats.
bips.impactMarkdown: BIP 88 is a tooling standard aimed at wallet developers. It has been used in some reference implementations though widespread adoption is pending.

bips.title: Chain Code Delegation
bips.summary: Proposes a delegation mechanism for BIP 32 chain codes, allowing limited key derivation rights to be granted to third parties.
bips.summaryMarkdown:
BIP 89 describes a technique for delegating chain code derivation authority without revealing the master private key. This enables use cases such as auditing where an external party needs to derive child public keys.

The chain code delegation supports hierarchical key management structures beyond the basic BIP 32 model.
bips.impactMarkdown: BIP 89 is in Draft status and has not seen widespread implementation. The concept addresses a real need in key management infrastructure but introduces complexity not yet adopted by most wallets.

bips.title: Buried Deployments
bips.summary: Documents buried deployment heights for BIP 34, BIP 65, and BIP 66, replacing version-bit signaling with hardcoded activation heights.
bips.summaryMarkdown:
BIP 90 describes buried deployments — soft forks so universally adopted they can be assumed as always-active. Instead of checking version bits, node software hardcodes activation heights: BIP 34 at block 227931, BIP 65 at block 388381, BIP 66 at block 363725.

This simplification reduces code complexity and treats mature deployments as part of the consensus baseline.
bips.impactMarkdown: BIP 90 was implemented in Bitcoin Core 0.15.0. The buried deployment approach is now standard practice for mature soft forks.

bips.title: Reduced threshold Segwit MASF
bips.summary: Specifies a reduced-threshold activation for SegWit using BIP 9 with an 80% miner signaling threshold instead of the original 95%.
bips.summaryMarkdown:
BIP 91 provides a fallback mechanism for SegWit activation using a lower miner threshold (80% instead of 95%). If the 95% threshold was not met, this mechanism would allow SegWit to activate with reduced miner support.

The BIP also required blocks to flag readiness for SegWit, creating a strong incentive for miners to signal support during the 2017 activation deadlock.
bips.impactMarkdown: BIP 91 never activated because the original BIP 9 deployment reached its 95% threshold first. However, its existence as a credible fallback is credited with breaking the activation logjam.

bips.title: codex32: Checksummed SSSS-aware BIP32 seeds
bips.summary: Defines codex32, a checksummed SSSS-aware BIP 32 seed format for secure offline backup and recovery.
authors: Leon Olsson Curr and Pearlwort Sneed
bips.summaryMarkdown: BIP 93 specifies the codex32 format for BIP 32 seeds: a 32-character encoded string with a Bech32-like checksum supporting Shamir’s Secret Sharing Scheme (SSSS). The format allows a seed to be split into multiple shares with threshold-based reconstruction.
bips.impactMarkdown: BIP 93 is in Draft status. The format has been discussed in wallet development circles but has not yet been widely adopted.

bips.title: Testnet 4
bips.summary: Creates Testnet 4, a new Bitcoin test network replacing Testnet 3 with a clean chain state and protection against easy coin generation.
bips.summaryMarkdown: BIP 94 specifies the launch of Testnet 4, addressing issues with Testnet 3 including excessive inflation from its 20-minute difficulty adjustment and an extremely long chain. Testnet 4 introduces modified difficulty adjustment preventing excessive coin generation and provides a clean genesis state for developers.
bips.impactMarkdown: Testnet 4 was activated in October 2023 and has become the primary test network for Bitcoin development, providing a more reliable testing environment than Testnet 3.

bips.title: Fast Merkle Trees
bips.summary: Defines a Fast Merkle Tree construction using SHA-256 midstate technique for more efficient block validation.
bips.summaryMarkdown: BIP 98 specifies a faster Merkle tree construction using the SHA-256 midstate technique. Traditional Merkle trees require two full SHA-256 compressions per leaf. The Fast Merkle Tree uses the midstate to reduce computational cost by approximately 30% while maintaining the same security guarantees.
bips.impactMarkdown: BIP 98 is a Draft proposal not yet deployed. The concept offers measurable performance improvements for block validation.

bips.title: Motivation and deployment of consensus rule changes ([soft/hard]forks)
bips.summary: Provides a taxonomy of consensus fork types and proposes deployment mechanisms for soft and hard forks on Bitcoin.
bips.summaryMarkdown:
BIP 99 creates a classification system for Bitcoin consensus rule changes, defining terminology for soft forks, hard forks, UASF, and MASF. It proposes a staged deployment process with milestones: announcement, implementation, signaling, lock-in, and activation.

The BIP aims to standardize how the community discusses and coordinates consensus changes.
bips.impactMarkdown: BIP 99 was closed as an active proposal, but many of its concepts entered common Bitcoin vocabulary during the SegWit activation debate of 2017.

bips.title: Dynamic maximum block size by miner vote
bips.summary: Proposes replacing the static 1 MB block size limit with a dynamic limit set by miner vote through the coinbase transaction.
bips.summaryMarkdown:
BIP 100 introduces a dynamic block size limit mechanism where miners vote on the maximum block size through their coinbase transactions. The proposed range allowed block sizes from 1 MB to 32 MB, with the limit determined by the 90th percentile of miner preferences.

This was intended to provide a market-driven approach to block space supply without requiring a hard fork for each adjustment.
bips.impactMarkdown: BIP 100 was one of several proposals during the 2015-2017 blocksize debate and was never adopted. The debate led to SegWit activation and the Bitcoin Cash fork. BIP 100 remains historically significant as a key proposal in that debate.
